answer:
Model the repair as an instance of E11 Modification (its scope note explicitly covers "the conservation treatment of an object"), linked to the six cabinets with P31 has modified. The question of who "carried out" it is then decided by one sentence in the P14 scope note: P14 carried out by "describes the active participation of an instance of E39 Actor in an instance of E7 Activity. It implies causal or legal responsibility." That test is about responsibility, not about whose hands touched the object. Two of your three people pass it; the third does not.

1. The two apprentices: P14 carried out by, each qualified with P14.1 in the role of an E55 Type such as "executant" / "conservation technician". They performed the filling, regluing and touch-up, which is active participation in the plainest sense.

2. The studio principal: also P14 carried out by, qualified with P14.1 in the role of "supervising conservator". She did not hold the brush, but she directed the work and signed it off, and the invoice is a statement of her responsibility for it. The CRM's own worked example for P14 is the painting of the Sistine Chapel "carried out by Michelangelo Buonaroti (E21) in the role of master craftsman (E55)" - a master-with-assistants attribution. The role qualifier exists precisely so that this kind of attribution can be made without pretending the master did every stroke.

3. So yes, more than one, and that is not a compromise - it is what the property is quantified for. P14's quantification is "many to many, necessary (1,n:0,n)": at least one actor must be recorded on an E11, and any number may be. What keeps the two attributions from collapsing into the false claim that all of them did the same thing is P14.1 in the role of (range E55 Type). When Martin Doerr addressed the employee-acting-for-an-employer form of this same question on the list, he prescribed exactly this construction - "We can use two P14 carried out by links" differing only in their P14.1 role (his terms were employer and implementer). Draw your role terms from a controlled vocabulary and keep them stable; Doerr's own caveat in that message was that such proposals should be documented and a good practice of role types collected, i.e. the CRM gives you the slot but not the terms.

4. The museum's conservation officer: do not put her on P14. She did none of the work and carried none of the responsibility for the treatment - the invoice puts that on the studio - so she fails both halves of the P14 test. Use its superproperty P11 had participant, which "implies that the actor was involved in the event but does not imply any causal relationship". This is exactly the boundary the SIG drew when the same doubt was raised about whether a baby carries out its own baptism: Doerr's ruling analogy was that "patients in a surgery are necessary, but do not carry it out", and Sanderson's conclusion was "as it's not P14, we should use P11 had participant". Note that the clarification proposed in that thread was never adopted - the v7.3.2 scope note for P14 is still just the two sentences quoted above - so the distinction rests on reading "active" and "responsibility" strictly rather than on any added wording.

Better still, give her a positive place of her own instead of only a weakened link to the treatment. Her two site visits are her own instances of E7 Activity, which she P14 carried out; and the museum's commissioning and oversight of the job is an overarching E7 Activity carried out by the museum (E74 Group) and by her, of which the workshop's E11 Modification P9i forms part. Doerr recommended precisely this partitioning for the acting-on-behalf-of case, preferring "forms part of" to any new property, on the grounds that "The \"part of\" implies the \"on behest of\"", and noting that it is monotonic in both directions: you can start from the individual activity and add the whole later, or start from the whole and add the sub-activity later.

5. Optionally a fourth carrier: if you want the invoice's own attribution in the data, the workshop itself (E74 Group) can take a further P14 carried out by on the same E11, in the role of contractor. It is the workshop that contracted, and it persists independently of which apprentices it employs. This is compatible with, not a substitute for, the individual attributions.

Limits you should know about. The CRM has no property that says "A worked under B's direction" or "A acted on behalf of B". Two issues were opened asking for one - issue 488 "Modelling an Actor carrying out an action at the Behest of Another", which got as far as a proposal about "subtyping P14.1 in the role of", and issue 542 "Groups and carried out by", which asked for a subproperty meaning carried out by member(s) of a group - and both were closed without adding anything, 542 because the SIG "resolved to discontinue work on CRMsoc" in April 2025 (it had been parked as "dependent on CRMsoc developments" in 2023). So the supervisor/executant asymmetry lives entirely in your own E55 Type role vocabulary, and a consumer who ignores P14.1 will see three or four actors who all equally "carried out" the repair. That flattening is inherent in the model as it stands; if the asymmetry must survive naive querying, use the partitioning instead - a supervising activity carried out by the principal, with the hands-on E11 forming part of it - so that the two attributions sit on different nodes.

One last honest note on the direction of doubt: the principal is the case that could be argued either way. If in some other engagement the named principal had merely lent her name to work she never saw, P11 would be the correct link for her and P14 would be an overstatement. Here she supervised and approved, so P14 is right. Do not reach for a one-person E74 Group standing for "the principal in her capacity as the studio" to finesse this; Doerr rejected that device because "there is no substance of identity to such a one-person Group", reserving it for offices and procurators.

rejected_alternatives.option: P11 had participant for the studio principal
rejected_alternatives.why_not: It would understate her. P11 'does not imply any causal relationship', but she directed the work and approved it, so she satisfies P14's test of 'causal or legal responsibility'. P11 is for involvement without responsibility.

rejected_alternatives.option: P14 carried out by for the museum's conservation officer
rejected_alternatives.why_not: She did none of the hands-on work and bore no responsibility for the treatment itself - the studio did. Doerr's analogy in the P14 'causal' thread rules this out: necessary or observing presence is not carrying out ('patients in a surgery are necessary, but do not carry it out').

rejected_alternatives.option: Recording only one actor, e.g. only the principal named on the invoice, or only the apprentices
rejected_alternatives.why_not: P14 is quantified 'many to many, necessary (1,n:0,n)', so multiple actors are the intended case, not an abuse. Recording only the principal loses who did the work; recording only the apprentices loses the responsibility the invoice asserts.

rejected_alternatives.option: A new or borrowed property meaning 'acted under the direction of' / 'on behalf of'
rejected_alternatives.why_not: No such property exists in CRMbase. Issue 488 and issue 542 both asked for one and both were closed without adding it, 542 when the SIG resolved to discontinue work on CRMsoc. Inventing one would put the answer outside the standard.

rejected_alternatives.option: E79 Part Addition / E80 Part Removal for the filling and regluing
rejected_alternatives.why_not: These subclasses of E11 are for activities whose point is that an identifiable part was added to or taken off a thing. Here the intervention is a single conservation treatment, which the E11 scope note names directly; splitting it into part-transactions would fragment the event and still not answer the actor question. Use them only if a specific added or removed part must be tracked.
Nothing new came into existence; the cabinets keep their identities. Production is the subclass reserved for activities that bring a thing into being.

rejected_alternatives.option: E10 Transfer of Custody for the treatment
rejected_alternatives.why_not: Not a rival - a complement. Sending the cabinets to the workshop and getting them back is a genuine pair of E10 events (custody moved, ownership did not), but an E10 is not the intervention and carries no P31 has modified.

rejected_alternatives.option: E14 Condition Assessment for the officer's two visits
rejected_alternatives.why_not: Right class only if she actually recorded a judgement about the cabinets' state, which the case does not say - she checked progress. If she did record findings, E14 (with P34 concerned) is the class, and she is its P14 actor; it is never the class for the repair.

rejected_alternatives.option: A one-person E74 Group representing 'the principal acting as the studio'
rejected_alternatives.why_not: Doerr rejected this device: 'there is no substance of identity to such a one-person Group', and it should be restricted to offices and procurators. Here the studio is a real group with employees, so use the group itself.

siblings_considered.why_not: E87 Curation Activity is the sibling a museum reader would reach for, since conservation is administered as part of collections care. But E87 is about managing an E78 Curated Holding - it is joined to holdings by P147 curated - and it has no way to say which physical thing was altered. The workshop changed the cabinets themselves, and only E11 carries P31 has modified. Record the museum's overall care programme as E87 if you wish, and let the treatment form part of it.

E74 Group could stand in for the people, and for the workshop that is right. But the whole point of the case is to distinguish who supervised from who executed, and a group attribution deliberately hides which member acted - the question raised in issue 542. All three named individuals are natural persons, so E21.

For the workshop and the museum, E21 Person is wrong: they are organisations acting collectively that persist independently of which individuals they currently employ, which is what E74's scope note covers. The named principal is a Person and is modelled separately from the studio she runs.

E89 Propositional Object is the closest sibling, and role terms like 'supervising conservator' are not sets of propositions documented as units - they are vocabulary concepts used to classify a participation. E55 Type is in any case the declared range of P14.1, so no sibling can substitute.

Honestly, no sibling of E7 is a plausible rival. The closest are E63 Beginning of Existence and E64 End of Existence, and neither applies: the officer's inspection visits and the museum's oversight of the commission bring nothing into existence and end nothing. E7 is simply the general class for intentional action, which is what these are.

notes: Two things the tools made awkward. (1) `concept P14` prints the v7.1.3 scope note; to be sure the 2022 proposal to rewrite it (thread t1546) had not been adopted I had to pull the v7.3.2 declaration with `docs --json`, which is also the only way to learn the doc chunk ids (crm732#P14 etc.) needed by `quote`. Plain `docs` output does not show them. (2) `concept E74` reports its sibling below the property blocks, so a truncated read makes E74 look sibling-less; E21 Person is its sibling. Substantively, the search system did put the decisive material on screen: the P14 scope note supplies the test, thread t1546 supplies the SIG's own reading of it, thread t1345 supplies both the multi-role and the activity-partitioning constructions from Doerr, and issues 488 and 542 establish that nothing more specific was ever added. The one thing I could not find is any guidance on what role terms to use - the CRM supplies the P14.1 slot and no vocabulary, and Doerr's message says as much.
